ACTIVE\_JOB\_INFO table function
IBMi 7.6 Query Performance Optimization.pdf
The ACTIVE\_JOB\_INFO table function returns one row for every active job.  
The information returned is similar to the detail seen from the Work with Active Jobs (WRKACTJOB) command and the List Job (QUSLJOB) API. The ACTIVE\_JOB\_INFO table function has two uses:  
1. To see details for all, or a subset of, active jobs. A subset of active jobs can be requested by using the optional filter parameters.  
2. To measure elapsed statistics for active jobs. You can use an optional parameter to reset statistics, similar to the WRKACTJOB command F10 Restart Statistics function. Measurements will be calculated based on this new starting point.  
Authorization: None required to see general information or to see information for jobs where the caller's user profile is the same as the job user identity of the job for which the information is being returned.  
For DETAILED\_INFO => NONE or DETAILED\_INFO => WORK :  
- None required.  
For DETAILED\_INFO => QTEMP :  
- The caller must have *JOBCTL special authority.  
For DETAILED\_INFO => ALL or FULL :  
- None required to see detailed column information for the columns that are included with DETAILED\_INFO => WORK or the CLIENT\_IP\_ADDRESS, PAGE\_FAULTS, PRESTART\_JOB\_REUSE\_COUNT, PRESTART\_JOB\_MAX\_USE\_COUNT, and WORKLOAD\_GROUP columns.
- A caller who is authorized to the QIBM\_DB\_SQLADM or QIBM\_DB\_SYSMON function usage identifiers can see detailed column information related to SQL activity starting with the SQL\_STATEMENT\_TEXT column through the PSEUDO\_CLOSED\_CURSOR\_COUNT column.
- A caller with *JOBCTL special authority can see all detailed column information.

```  
Note: The data in the ELAPSED\_xxx columns is updated upon each re-execution of the query. Elapsed data will not get returned the first time a query is run for ACTIVE\_JOB\_INFO for a connection. See the reset-statistics parameter for details.  
- Example 2: Find the active jobs using the most temporary storage. Include the most recently executed SQL statement for each target job.

```

---

REPLY\_INQUIRY\_MESSAGES scalar function
IBMi 7.6 Query Performance Optimization.pdf
The REPLY\_INQUIRY\_MESSAGES scalar function replies to one or more inquiry messages in the QSYSOPR message queue.  
This function extends what can be done by the Send Reply (SNDRPY) CL command.  
Authorization:  
See Note below.  
<!-- image -->  
The schema is SYSTOOLS.  
message-id  
A character string containing the message identifier of the inquiry message. The special value *IMMED can be specified to indicate the message has no message identifier.  
search- message-text  
A character string containing a string that must exist in the message text in order for the inquiry message to be selected. The comparison is case insensitive.  
When message-id is *IMMED, a value must be specified. Otherwise, a value is optional.  
response  
A character string containing the response to be provided to any inquiry messages that meet the message-id and search-string criteria.  
If response is omitted or contains the value *DFT, the default reply stored in the message description of the inquiry message is sent as the reply, or the system default reply of *N is used.  
remove- message  
A character string that indicates whether the inquiry message and its reply are removed from the message queue.  
NO The message will not be removed.  
YES The message will be removed. This is the default.  
The result of the function is an integer that indicates the number of inquiry messages that were responded to.

---

Replying to Run-Time Inquiry Messages
IBMi 7.6 ILE RPG Programmers Guide.pdf
When you run a program with ILE RPG procedures, run-time inquiry messages may be generated. They occur when the default error handler is invoked for a function check in a cycle-main procedure. See 'Exception Handling within a Cycle-Main Procedure' on page 329. The inquiry messages require a response before the program continues running.  
Note: Inquiry messages are never issued for subprocedures (including those designated as linear-main procedures), since the default error handling for a function check in a subprocedure causes the subprocedure to be cancelled, causing the exception to percolate to the caller of the subprocedure. See Exception Handling within Subprocedures.  
If the caller of the subprocedure is an RPG procedure, the call will fail with status 00202, independent of the status code associated with the actual exception. If the failed call causes an RPG cycle-main procedure to invoke its default handler, inquiry message RNQ0202 will be issued.  
You can add the inquiry messages to a system reply list to provide automatic replies to the messages. The replies for these messages may be specified individually or generally. This method of replying to inquiry messages is especially suitable for batch programs, which would otherwise require an operator to issue replies.  
To find all the ILE RPG inquiry messages you can add to the system reply list, use the following command:  
```
DSPMSGD RANGE(RNQ0100 RNQ9999) MSGF(QRNXMSG) DETAIL(*BASIC) OUTPUT(*PRINT)
```  
Note: ILE RPG inquiry messages have a message id prefix of RNQ.  
To add inquiry messages to a system reply list using the Add Reply List Entry command enter:  
```
ADDRPYLE sequence-no message-id
```  
where sequence-no is a number from 1-9999, which reflects where in the list the entry is being added, and message-id is the message number you want to add. Repeat this command for each message you want to add.  
Use the Change Job (CHGJOB) command (or other CL job command) to indicate that your job uses the reply list for inquiry messages. To do this, you should specify *SYSRPYL for the Inquiry Message Reply (INQMSGRPY) attribute.  
The reply list is only used when an inquiry message is sent by a job that has the Inquiry Message Reply (INQMSGRPY) attribute specified as INQMSGRPY(*SYSRPYL). The INQMSGRPY parameter occurs on the following CL commands:  
- Change Job (CHGJOB)
- Change Job Description (CHGJOBD)  
- Create Job Description (CRTJOBD)
- Submit Job (SBMJOB).  
You can also use the Work with Reply List Entry (WRKRPYLE) command to change or remove entries in the system reply list. For details of the ADDRPYLE and WRKRPYLE commands, see the CL and APIs section of the Programming category in IBM Documentation at this web site: https://www.ibm.com/docs/i.

---

Control the default reply to the query governor inquiry message
IBMi 7.6 Query Performance Optimization.pdf
The system administrator can control whether the interactive user has the option of ignoring the database query inquiry message by using the Change Job (CHGJOB) CL command.  
Changes made include the following:  
- If a value of *DFT is specified for the INQMSGRPY parameter of the Change Job (CHGJOB) CL command, the interactive user does not see the inquiry messages. The query is canceled immediately.
- If a value of *RQD is specified for the INQMSGRPY parameter of the Change Job (CHGJOB) CL command, the interactive user sees the inquiry. The user must reply to the inquiry.
- If a value of *SYSRPYL is specified for the INQMSGRPY parameter of the Change Job (CHGJOB) CL command, a system reply list is used to determine whether the interactive user sees the inquiry and whether a reply is necessary. The system reply list entries can be used to customize different default replies based on user profile name, user id, or process names. The fully qualified job name is available in the message data for inquiry message CPA4259. This algorithm allows the keyword CMPDTA to be used to select the system reply list entry that applies to the process or user profile. The user profile name is 10 characters long and starts at position 51. The process name is 10 character long and starts at position 27.
- The following example adds a reply list element that causes the default reply of C to cancel requests for jobs whose user profile is 'QPGMR'.  
```
ADDRPYLE  SEQNBR(56) MSGID(CPA4259) CMPDTA(QPGMR      51) RPY(C)
```  
The following example adds a reply list element that causes the default reply of C to cancel requests for jobs whose process name is 'QPADEV0011'.  
```
ADDRPYLE  SEQNBR(57) MSGID(CPA4259) CMPDTA(QPADEV0011 27) RPY(C)
```

IBMi 7.6 Globalization.pdf

Handling messages with a specific object-level CCSID  
These listed objects support CCSIDs. Each of them has an object-level CCSID.  
- Message files
- Message queues
- Job message queues
- System reply lists
- History log  
The object-level CCSID is the CCSID in which all the messages in that object are encoded.  
Object-level coded character set identifier 65535  
CCSID 65535 is the default object-level CCSID for message files and message queues.  
If an object has a CCSID of 65535, no conversions occur when adding messages to that object or when receiving messages from that object. Use CCSID 65535 if you do not want CCSID processing to occur.  
CCSID 65535 is also known as *HEX.

Command : End Job (ENDJOB)
IBMi 7.6 Work management.pdf
If you do not know the name of the job that you want to end, you can use one of the following commands to find the job name:  
- Work with Active Jobs (WRKACTJOB)
- Work with User Jobs (WRKUSRJOB)
- Work with Submitted Jobs (WRKSBMJOB)

- End Subsystem (ENDSBS) This command ends all of the jobs in the subsystem.
- End System (ENDSYS) This command ends most activity on the system and leaves the system in a condition in which only the console is active in the controlling subsystem.
- Power Down System (PWRDWNSYS) This command prepares the system for ending and then starts the power-down sequence.  
A job may be ended either immediately or in a controlled manner. It is strongly recommended that you always attempt to end a job in a controlled manner.

---

Options to view thread information
IBMi 7.6 Multithreaded Programming.pdf
You can use the Display Job (DSPJOB) , Work with Job (WRKJOB) , and Work with Active Jobs (WRKACTJOB) commands to display and work with threads associated with an IBM i job.  
Through each of these commands, you can select an option that you can use to display or work with the threads in the job. You can use the Work with Threads display to view the following information for the job:  
- List of threads  
This display shows all of the threads that are currently associated with the job. The first thread in the list is the initial thread in the process. This list changes depending on the thread activity in the job. The 8-digit number is the thread identifier. Other information about this display includes the thread's status of active or waiting, total CPU usage, total auxiliary storage I/O counts, and thread run priority.  
- Thread call stack option  
This option displays the call stack of any thread. In some conditions, typically when the thread is running an instruction that cannot be interrupted, the call stack cannot be displayed. In these cases, a message indicating that no stack information is available is displayed.  
- Thread mutual exclusions (mutexes) option  
You can use this option to see all mutexes associated with a specific thread. This includes mutexes that are held and the mutex for which the thread might be waiting. If the specified thread has no mutexes associated with it, no mutex is displayed for the thread.  
- Thread locks option  
You can use this option to see all the thread-scoped object locks held by the thread. You can also use this option to see all pending process-scoped locks and thread-scoped locks on which the thread is waiting. If the specified thread has no object locks associated with it, there is no lock displayed for the thread.  
- Hold thread option  
You can use this option to temporarily suspend the running of a specific thread. This option is useful if you suspect that a thread might be looping or causing some other system problems. You must use the Hold thread option in conjunction with the Release thread option. Unlike Hold Job (HLDJOB) ,  
repeated Hold thread requests are cumulative. To resume the running of a held thread, you must issue the equivalent number of release thread requests.  
- Release thread option  
You can use this option to resume the running of a thread that was suspended.  
- End thread option  
You can use this option to end a specific thread. In general, you must not use this option because it can cause unpredictable results. This option requires *SERVICE special authority.  
The Release Job (RLSJOB) , Hold Job (HLDJOB) , End Job (ENDJOB) , and End Job Abnormal (ENDJOBABN) commands affect all threads within a multithreaded job. No commands are planned to provide the equivalent thread-level support.

data.content:
End Job  (ENDJOB)
**Where allowed to run:** All environments (*ALL)  
**Threadsafe:** No 

The End Job (ENDJOB) command ends the specified job and any associated inline data files. The job can be on a job queue, it can be active, or it can have already completed running. 

You can specify that the application program is given time to control end-of-job processing. If no time is given or if cleanup cannot be performed within the given time, the system performs minimal end-of-job processing, which can include: 

* Closing the database files.
* Spooling the job log to an output queue.
* Cleaning up internal objects in the operating system.
* Showing the end-of-job display (for interactive jobs).
* Completing commitment control processing  
Before ending the job, you should verify that no logical unit of work is in an in doubt state due to a two-phase commit operation that is in progress. If it is, then the value of the Action if ENDJOB commitment option can greatly impact the ENDJOB processing. For example, if the Action if ENDJOB commitment option is the default value of WAIT, this job will be held up and will not complete its end of job processing until the commitment control operation is completed. This ensures database integrity on all related systems. For specific instructions on how to determine these conditions, and for a description of all the impacts of ending this job under these conditions, see the Backup and Recovery book.

**Restrictions:** The issuer of the command must be running under a user profile which is the same as the job user identity of the job being ended, or the issuer of the command must be running under a user profile which has job control (*JOBCTL) special authority. This restriction is enforced even when ending the current job. 

The job user identity is the name of the user profile by which a job is known to other jobs. It is described in more detail in the Work Management book.

Parameter Overview
| Keyword                              | Description                 | Choices                                            | Notes                  |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| [**JOB**](#ENDJOB.JOB)               | Job name                    | Single values: *Other values: _Qualified job name_ | Required, Positional 1 |
| Qualifier 1: Job name                | _Name_                      |                                                    |                        |
| Qualifier 2: User                    | _Name_                      |                                                    |                        |
| Qualifier 3: Number                  | 000000-999999               |                                                    |                        |
| [**OPTION**](#ENDJOB.OPTION)         | How to end                  | ***CNTRLD**, *IMMED                                | Optional, Positional 2 |
| [**DELAY**](#ENDJOB.DELAY)           | Controlled end delay time   | 1-999999, **30**                                   | Optional, Positional 3 |
| [**SPLFILE**](#ENDJOB.SPLFILE)       | Delete spooled files        | ***NO**, *YES                                      | Optional, Positional 4 |
| [**LOGLMT**](#ENDJOB.LOGLMT)         | Maximum log entries         | _Integer_, ***SAME**, *NOMAX                       | Optional               |
| [**ADLINTJOBS**](#ENDJOB.ADLINTJOBS) | Additional interactive jobs | ***NONE**, *GRPJOB, *ALL                           | Optional               |
| [**DUPJOBOPT**](#ENDJOB.DUPJOBOPT)   | Duplicate job option        | ***SELECT**, *MSG                                  | Optional               |


JOB
### Job name (JOB)

Specifies the qualified job name of the job to be ended. 

This is a required parameter. 

**Single values** 

*****

The job from which this command is run is ended. Specifying this value is the only way to end the current job. 

**Qualifier 1: Job name** 

**_name_**

Specify the name of the job. 

**Qualifier 2: User** 

**_name_**

Specify the user name that identifies the user profile under which the job is run. 

**Qualifier 3: Number** 

**_000000-999999_**

Specify the system-assigned job number. 

**Note:** If no user name or job number is specified, all jobs currently in the system are searched for the job name. If more than one occurrence of the specified name is found, a qualified job name must be provided either explicitly or through the selection display. Refer to the **Duplicate job option (DUPJOBOPT)** parameter for more information.


Qualifier 1: Job name



Qualifier 2: User



Qualifier 3: Number



OPTION
### How to end (OPTION)

Specifies whether the job ends immediately or in a controlled manner that lets the application program perform end-of-job processing. In either case, the system performs certain job cleanup processing. 

***CNTRLD**

The job ends in a controlled manner. This allows the program running to perform cleanup (end-of-job processing). When a job being ended has a signal handling procedure for the asynchronous signal SIGTERM, the SIGTERM signal is generated for that job. The application has the amount of time specified on the DELAY parameter to complete cleanup before the job is ended. 

***IMMED**

The job ends immediately and the system performs end-of-job cleanup. System cleanup can take from a brief amount of time to several minutes. When a job being ended has a signal handling procedure for the asynchronous signal SIGTERM, the SIGTERM signal is generated for that job and the QENDJOBLMT system value specifies the time limit. Other than by handling the SIGTERM signal, the program that is running is not allowed to perform any cleanup. 

**Note:** The *IMMED value might cause undesirable results if data has been partially updated. This value should be used only after a controlled end has been attempted unsuccessfully. 

**Note:** When a SIGTERM signal handler is running during the immediate ending of a job, an ENDJOB command with OPTION(*IMMED) can be used to end the SIGTERM signal handler. This is only allowed if the SIGTERM signal handler has already had at least two minutes to run.


DELAY
### Controlled end delay time (DELAY)

Specifies the amount of time (in seconds) allowed for the job to complete its cleanup processing during a controlled end. If the cleanup is not completed before the end of the delay time, the job is ended immediately. (Only system cleanup is performed.) 

The delay time does not start until the job becomes active if the job is suspended because of one of the following conditions: 

* The system request option 1 is selected.
* The job is held by the Hold Job (HLDJOB) command.
* The job is transferred by the Transfer Secondary Job (TFRSECJOB) command.
* The job is transferred by the Transfer to Group Job (TFRGRPJOB) command.

**Note:** This parameter is valid only when OPTION(*CNTRLD) is specified. 

**30**

A maximum delay time of 30 seconds is allowed for cleanup before the job ends. 

**_1-999999_**

Specify the maximum amount of delay time (in seconds) before the job ends.


SPLFILE
### Delete spooled files (SPLFILE)

Specifies whether spooled output files created by this job are kept for normal processing or deleted. Regardless of whether the spooled files are deleted, the job logs are kept. 

***NO**

The spooled output files created by the job being ended are kept for normal processing by a writer. When the job ends, the spooled file action (SPLFACN) job attribute determines whether spooled files are detached from the job or kept with the job. 

***YES**

The spooled output files created by the job being ended and which are on output queues in the library name space of the thread issuing this command are deleted. The job log is not deleted. If the job has already ended and the spooled file action for the job is to detach the spooled files, the End Job (ENDJOB) command will not find the job and the spooled files will not be deleted.


LOGLMT
### Maximum log entries (LOGLMT)

Specifies the maximum number of entries in the message queue of the job being ended that are written to the job log. This parameter can be used to limit the number of messages written to the job log printer file, QPJOBLOG, for a job that ends. 

The value specified on this parameter can change the logging limit of the job even if the job is already ending or the job has already ended. The following are examples of how the logging limit can be changed: 

1. If the value specified is greater than the number of messages written at the time the command is issued, messages continue to be written until the new limit is reached.
2. If the value specified is less than the number of messages already written to the spooled file, a message indicating that the limit has been reached is immediately put in the spooled file as the last entry. The remaining messages on the queue are ignored.
3. If 0 (zero) is specified before any messages are written to the spooled file, no job log is produced for the job that is ending. If the job has already ended and the job log has not yet been produced, the job log is removed regardless of the value of the job log output (LOGOUTPUT) job attribute. For more information on removing pending job logs, refer to the Remove Pending Job Log (QWTRMVJL) API.

***SAME**

The message logging limit does not change. If the logging limit does not change for this job on a previous command, *NOMAX is the value used by the system. 

***NOMAX**

There is no limit to the number of messages logged; **all** messages on the job message queue are written to the job log. 

**_integer-number_**

Specify the maximum number of messages that can be written to the job log.


ADLINTJOBS
### Additional interactive jobs (ADLINTJOBS)

Specifies whether the additional interactive jobs associated with the job specified in the **Job name (JOB)** parameter are ended. 

***NONE**

Only the job specified in the JOB parameter is ended. 

***GRPJOB**

If the job specified in the JOB parameter is a group job, all group jobs associated with the group are ended. If the job is not a group job, the job specified in the JOB parameter is ended. 

***ALL**

All interactive jobs running on the workstation associated with the job specified in the JOB parameter are ended. This includes group jobs and secondary jobs.


DUPJOBOPT
### Duplicate job option (DUPJOBOPT)

Specifies the action taken when duplicate jobs are found by this command. 

***SELECT**

The selection display is shown when duplicate jobs are found during an interactive session. Otherwise, a message is issued. 

***MSG**

A message is issued when duplicate jobs are found.


Examples
**Example 1: Ending a Job Immediately** 


ENDJOB   JOB(JOB1)  OPTION(*IMMED)  SPLFILE(*YES)

This command ends a job named JOB1 immediately. Spooled output produced by the job is deleted; the job log is saved. 

**Example 2: Saving Spooled Output** 


ENDJOB   JOB(001234/XYZ/JOB2)  OPTION(*CNTRLD)
         DELAY(50)  SPLFILE(*NO)

This command ends a job named 001234/XYZ/JOB2\. Spooled output is saved for normal processing by the spooling writer. The job has 50 seconds to perform any cleanup routines, after which it is ended immediately. 

**Example 3: Removing a Pending Job Log** 


ENDJOB   JOB(543210/ABCDE/JOB3)  LOGLMT(0)

This command removes the pending job log for a completed job named 543210/ABCDE/JOB3\. This has the same effect as the Remove Pending Job Log (QWTRMVJL) API. 

**Example 4: Ending the Current Job** 


ENDJOB   JOB(*)  OPTION(*IMMED)

This command ends the job in which the command is issued. To exit from a SIGTERM signal handling procedure after the required cleanup has been performed, immediately end the current job. Control may be returned to the command issuer, even though the immediate option has been used. To handle this situation, the program which issued this command should return.


Error Messages
***ESCAPE Messages** 

**CPF1317**

No response from subsystem for job &3/&2/&1\. 

**CPF1321**

Job &1 user &2 job number &3 not found. 

**CPF1332**

End of duplicate job names. 

**CPF1340**

Job control function not performed. 

**CPF1341**

Reader or writer &3/&2/&1 not allowed as job name.

data.content:
Hold Job  (HLDJOB)
**Where allowed to run:** All environments (*ALL)  
**Threadsafe:** No 

The Hold Job (HLDJOB) command makes a job ineligible for processing by the system. The job is held until it is: 

* Released by the Release Job (RLSJOB) command
* Cleared by the Clear Job Queue (CLRJOBQ) command
* Ended by the End Job (ENDJOB) command
* Ended (while the job is active) by the End Subsystem (ENDSBS) command, the End System (ENDSYS) command, or the Power Down System (PWRDWNSYS) command

Holding a job causes all threads within the job to be held. 

**Note:** If you use this command to hold a job that has exclusive access to any resources on the system, these resources are not available to other jobs. Other jobs which require access to those resources will either fail or wait indefinitely. 

**Restrictions:** The issuer of the command must be running under a user profile which is the same as the job user identity of the job being held, or the issuer of the command must be running under a user profile which has job control (*JOBCTL) special authority. 

The job user identity is the name of the user profile by which a job is known to other jobs. It is described in more detail in the Work Management book.

Parameter Overview
| Keyword                            | Description          | Choices              | Notes                  |
| ---------------------------------- | -------------------- | -------------------- | ---------------------- |
| [**JOB**](#HLDJOB.JOB)             | Job name             | _Qualified job name_ | Required, Positional 1 |
| Qualifier 1: Job name              | _Name_               |                      |                        |
| Qualifier 2: User                  | _Name_               |                      |                        |
| Qualifier 3: Number                | 000000-999999        |                      |                        |
| [**SPLFILE**](#HLDJOB.SPLFILE)     | Hold spooled files   | ***NO**, *YES        | Optional, Positional 2 |
| [**DUPJOBOPT**](#HLDJOB.DUPJOBOPT) | Duplicate job option | ***SELECT**, *MSG    | Optional               |


JOB
### Job name (JOB)

Specifies the name of the job being held. 

This is a required parameter. 

**Qualifier 1: Job name** 

**_name_**

Specify the name of the job. 

**Qualifier 2: User** 

**_name_**

Specify the user name that identifies the user profile under which the job is started. 

**Qualifier 3: Number** 

**_000000-999999_**

Specify the system-assigned job number. 

**Note:** If no user name or job number is specified, all jobs currently in the system are searched for the job name. If more than one occurrence of the specified name is found, a qualified job name must be provided either explicitly or through the selection display. Refer to the **Duplicate job option (DUPJOBOPT)** parameter for more information.


Qualifier 1: Job name



Qualifier 2: User



Qualifier 3: Number



SPLFILE
### Hold spooled files (SPLFILE)

Specifies whether spooled output files created by the job being held are also held. 

***NO**

The spooled output files produced by the job are not held. 

***YES**

The spooled output files produced by the job are also held. Only those spooled output files which are on output queues in the library name space of the thread issuing this command will be held. If the **Spooled file action (SPLFACN)** job attribute is *DETACH and the job is ended while the spooled files are held, the spooled files cannot be released using the Release Job (RLSJOB) command. To release spooled files after the job has been removed from the system, use the Release Spooled File (RLSSPLF) command.


DUPJOBOPT
### Duplicate job option (DUPJOBOPT)

Specifies the action taken when duplicate jobs are found by this command. 

***SELECT**

The selection display is shown when duplicate jobs are found during an interactive session. Otherwise, a message is issued. 

***MSG**

A message is issued when duplicate jobs are found.


Examples
**Example 1: Making a Job Ineligible for Processing** 


HLDJOB   JOB(PAYROLL)  SPLFILE(*YES)

This command makes the job named PAYROLL ineligible for processing. All spooled files for this job are also held. 

**Example 2: Holding a Job that has a Duplicate Name** 


HLDJOB   JOB(DEPTXYZ/PAYROLL)

This command holds the job named PAYROLL submitted by a user operating under the user profile DEPTXYZ. The qualified form of the job name is used when jobs with duplicate names exist in the system. Spooled files are not held.

**CPF1345**

**CPF1347**

     A*   MSGSFL    - Subfile: one row per MSGW job

     A*   FOOTER    - Function key legend (OVERLAY)

     A*   MSGQCTL   - Message subfile control
     A*===========================================================================

     A*---------------------------------------------------------------------------
     A* File-level keywords
     A*---------------------------------------------------------------------------
     A                                      DSPSIZ(24 80 *DS3)
     A                                      INDARA
     A                                      CF03(03 'Exit')
     A                                      CF05(05 'Refresh')
     A                                      CF12(12 'Cancel')
     A*
     A*---------------------------------------------------------------------------
     A* MSGSFL - Subfile record format (one row per MSGW job)
     A*---------------------------------------------------------------------------
     A          R MSGSFL                    SFL
     A*
     A* Option field (input): 2=Work with Job, 3=Hold, 4=End Job (Cntrl),
     A*   5=Display Messages, 6=Release, 7=Display Job Log, 8=End Job (Immed)
     A            SFOPT          3A  B  5  2

     A            SFJOBUSR      10A  O  5 13
     A            SFJOBNAM      10A  O  5 24
     A*
     A* Job type and subsystem
     A            SFJOBTYP       3A  O  5 35
     A            SFSUBSYS      10A  O  5 39
     A*
     A* Function information (what the job is doing)
     A            SFTYPE         2A  O  5 50
     A            SFFUNCTION    10A  O  5 53
     A*
     A* Hidden field: full qualified job name (nnnnnnn/user/jobname)
     A            SFQJOB        28A  H

     A*---------------------------------------------------------------------------
     A          R MSGCTL                    SFLCTL(MSGSFL)

data.content:
Now I understand the errors:

1. **Line 104** — the "no-records" constant `'No jobs currently in MSGW status.'` inside the subfile control record is at position 20, column 5, conditioned on indicator 33. The DDS compiler says "Plus sign in position value required when no line number" — the conditional constants in subfile control records need the indicator to precede the line/position. The `COLOR(GRN)` on the continuation line after a conditioned constant is also invalid — `COLOR` on constants requires them to be on the same line as the literal, but the continuation line error is because `COLOR` is not valid for output literals with conditioning in `SFLCTL`. I'll move the text to a named output field instead, so we can give it color.

2. **CPD7484** — `COLOR` is **not valid for named constants** (literals) in the subfile control record. It's only valid for named fields. I need to make the footer constants simple (no `COLOR`) or use named fields. Actually `COLOR` IS valid on constant (unnamed) fields in DDS display files — the issue is that the error is on **line 104** specifically, which is the conditional constant. This is actually a known DDS restriction: **COLOR is not valid on conditional constants** in SFLCTL (they must be unconditional or put in a separate record).

3. **CPD7848** on line 151 — `SFLPGMQ` specified in both the subfile record (`MSGQSFL`) AND the subfile control record (`MSGQCTL`). Per IBM DDS rules for message subfiles with `SFLMSGRCD`, `SFLPGMQ` in the control record is only needed when `SFLINZ` is used. Since we don't use `SFLINZ`, we should remove `SFLPGMQ` from `MSGQCTL`.

The `NOMSGFLD` field has wrong formatting. In DDS, for a named field in a subfile control record, position 19 is where the field name starts (positions 19-28). The name `NOMSGFLD` (8 chars) starts at position 19. Let me check the exact column layout. The error says "Position 18 must be blank" — this means my field definition line has something in position 18, but position 18 should be blank (it's the "reserved" column between the field usage and the line/position). Let me look at the exact DDS column layout for field entries:

- Positions 19-28: Field name
- Position 29: Reference 
- Positions 30-34: Length
- Position 35: Data type
- Positions 36-37: Decimal positions
- Position 38: Usage (I/O/B/H/M/P)
- Positions 39-41: Line
- Positions 42-44: Position
- Positions 45-80: Keywords

The problem is that in the DDS source I wrote `A  33       NOMSGFLD      34A  O 20  5COLOR(GRN)` — the field definition has the indicator in positions 7-8, and `NOMSGFLD` in positions 19-28, `34` in positions 30-34 (length), `A` in position 35, space in 36-37, `O` in position 38, `20` in 39-41, `5` in 42-44. But position 18 contains something when using option indicators. Let me check — with indicator 33 in positions 7-8, positions 9-16 are blank (no AND/OR), positions 17-18 blank, position 19 starts the name. Actually the issue is that the `NOMSGFLD` name should start at column 19 in the source, but I need to look at how many spaces precede it.

The standard column ruler for DDS is:
```
         1         2         3         4         5         6         7
1234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890
```
- Col 7-8: Option indicators
- Col 9-10: 2nd indicator
- Col 11-12: 3rd indicator  
- Col 17: Type of name (blank=field, R=record format)
- Col 18: Reserved (must be blank for field entries)
- Col 19-28: Field name

Looking at the output listing earlier for the subfile record, the SFOPT field is formatted as:
```
     A            SFOPT          3A  B  5  2
```
That's `12 spaces` + `SFOPT` + spaces. Let me count:
- Columns 1-6: `     A` (6 chars)
- Col 7: blank (no indicator)
- Col 8: blank
- Col 9-16: blank  
- Col 17: blank (field type = blank = field name)
- Col 18: blank
- Col 19-28: `SFOPT     ` (name, padded to 10 chars)

So `     A            SFOPT` = 6 + 12 spaces + name. But my line `A  33       NOMSGFLD` has:
- `     A` (col 1-6)
- `  33` (col 7-10, indicator 33 in positions 7-8 = `33` but that means col 7='3' and col 8='3')
- Then spaces up to col 19

Wait — the indicator format in DDS is: positions 7, 8 (1st indicator), 9 (NOT), 10-11 (2nd indicator), 12 (NOT), 13-14 (3rd indicator), 15 (NOT), 16 blank. Then 17=type, 18=reserved, 19-28=name.

Looking at the SFLCLR line in the compiled output: `A  33       SFLCLR` — that has `33` starting at position 7. But for a record-level keyword like SFLCLR, those indicators are at the record level, and position 17 determines if it's a field name. For my named field with indicator conditioning, the format should be:

`     A  33        NOMSGFLD      34A  O 20  5COLOR(GRN)`

Where positions 7-8=`33`, 9-18=spaces (10 spaces), 19-28=`NOMSGFLD  `. Let me re-examine the column positions more carefully. The error "Position 18 must be blank" means something is at position 18.

The simplest fix: remove the `NOMSGFLD` output field approach and instead just put the "no records" message in the FOOTER record (always shown), or eliminate the color on it entirely:

The errors are still on the `COLOR` keywords in the `FOOTER` record and on the "no jobs" constant line (now line 108). The error "Value in indicated numeric field not allowed" at column 42 is in the `20  5` position — with a conditioning indicator (`33`) before a constant, the constant *must* come on the same line as the indicator in positions 39-41 and 42-44. Also, the `COLOR` keywords in the `FOOTER` record — "Keyword not valid for this file type" — means `COLOR` is NOT valid for unnamed constants (literals) in display files.

Let me check IBM documentation on whether `COLOR` can be used with unnamed field constants:

From the DDS skill: `COLOR` usage is `COLOR(color)` at field level. But **unnamed constants (literals)** in DDS don't support `COLOR` — they only support `DSPATR`. This is a well-known DDS limitation. For colored text, you must use **named output fields** (`O` usage) and set them from the RPG program.

For the "no jobs" message, I'll move it to the RPG program and display it via the message subfile instead.

For the FOOTER — just remove COLOR from the constants since the function key legend doesn't need to be colored. I'll keep `DSPATR(HI)` if needed instead.

Also the "Value in indicated numeric field not allowed" at line 108 col 42 — this is the `20  5` (line 20, position 5) for the "no jobs" constant, conditioned by indicator 33. The DDS restriction for conditional constants in SFLCTL: when using option indicators for a constant literal within a subfile control record, the literal line/pos must be on the same line as the indicator. My DDS `A  33                              20  5'No jobs...'` — let me count columns:

```
     A  33                              20  5'No jobs currently in MSGW status.'
123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890
         1         2         3         4         5
```
- Positions 1-5: spaces
- Position 6: `A`
- Position 7-8: `33` (indicator)
- Positions 9-38: spaces (30 spaces)
- Positions 39-41: `20 ` (line number — but this is 3 chars for line, and the ` ` is needed)

Wait, actually positions 39-41 is the line number and 42-44 is the position. So for `20  5`:
- `20 ` would be in positions 39-41 (line=20)
- ` 5 ` in positions 42-44 (pos=5, right-justified means ` 5`)

Hmm. `20  5'No jobs...'` — that would be `20` in 39-40, space in 41, space in 42, `5` in 43, `'No jobs...'` starts at 45.

The error "Value in indicated numeric field not allowed" at column 42 suggests that column 42-44 has invalid content. The value `  5` should work for position 5... unless the line number `20` goes into positions 39-41 only if padded: `20 ` = `2`, `0`, ` `. OK that's line 20. Then positions 42-44 = `  5` = blank, blank, 5. Column 42 is blank. Error at column 42... 

I think the real issue here is that in the FOOTER record (which does NOT have SFLSIZ/SFLPAG), the conditional constant `A  33  ...  20  5` is simply causing multiple errors.

The simplest clean approach: **move everything out of FOOTER that needs color or conditioning** and just put simple constants there with no attributes. The "no jobs" message will be sent via the message subfile from RPG. This is actually cleaner.

Also, I realize the issue with `COLOR` on constants in FOOTER: the DDS compiler says `COLOR` is **not valid on constants** in a non-subfile display file record. Constants only support `DSPATR` attributes, not `COLOR`. This is confirmed by the "Keyword not valid for this file type" errors.

Let me rewrite the DDS completely with these rules applied:

But also, `chain` to a subfile uses the subfile record name. The issue is that `CHAIN` to a subfile format in an WORKSTN file should use `chain WkRRN MSGSFL` (which is correct for subfiles), but `%found` needs the **file** name. However, looking at the error: "Factor 2 is not a WORKSTN subfile-format name" for the CHAIN — this means `CHAIN` is not valid with a WORKSTN subfile format! For display files, you use `READC` (read changed) to read subfile rows that were modified, not `CHAIN`.

2. **Line 360**: Same issue with `update MSGSFL` — "Factor 2 is not a WORKSTN subfile-format name" — actually `UPDATE` should be valid on subfile formats. Let me re-check: in free-format, `update MSGSFL;` should work. But the format name in the free-format `chain`/`update` needs to be the record format name as declared by the DCL-F. Wait — the error says "Factor 2 is not a WORKSTN subfile-format name" which means the format isn't recognized as a subfile.

The fundamental issue with the `CHAIN` operation: in ILE RPG with a WORKSTN file, you use `CHAIN(n) recformat` where `n` is the RRN for subfiles. The proper way to do it:

```rpg
// Read specific RRN from subfile
chain WkRRN MSGSFL;
```

But the error says "Factor 2 is not a WORKSTN subfile-format name." This could be because the format name `MSGSFL` isn't being found. Actually, in free-form RPG, CHAIN to a subfile record format should work. Let me check — the file `MSGWDSPF` has record formats `MSGSFL`, `MSGCTL`, `FOOTER`, `MSGQSFL`, `MSGQCTL`. The `chain` should use the subfile format name `MSGSFL`.

Looking more carefully at the error: "Factor 2 is not a WORKSTN subfile-format name" — this is for `CHAIN`. In fixed-form RPG, reading a subfile record by RRN uses `CHAIN` with the RRN in factor 1 and the format name in factor 2. In **free-format RPG**, the syntax is also `chain key file/format`. But maybe the issue is that for a WORKSTN file, `CHAIN` to a subfile record format for **reading** (not for I/O) is being complained about.

Actually, the correct approach for iterating through a subfile to find entered options is to use **READC** (read changed records). This reads all subfile records where the operator entered data (modified data tag is set). That's much more efficient than chaining to each RRN.

For `UPDATE` to a subfile — this IS valid. The error on line 360 about `UPDATE MSGSFL` is strange. Let me look at line 360 in the source more carefully.

Actually: the file is declared as `dcl-f MSGWDSPF workstn indds(Ind);`. For a WORKSTN file with a subfile, CHAIN to read a specific RRN should work. ## MSGWMON — Real-Time MSGW Job Monitor

### What was built

Two source members in `BOB4IPGMR`:

| Object | Library | Type | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`MSGWDSPF`](BOB4IPGMR/QDSPFSRC/MSGWDSPF.DSPF) | BOB4IPGMR | *FILE DSPF | `QDSPFSRC,MSGWDSPF` |
| [`MSGWMON`](BOB4IPGMR/QRPGLESRC/MSGWMON.SQLRPGLE) | BOB4IPGMR | *PGM RPGLE | `QRPGLESRC,MSGWMON` |

---

### Screen Layout (80×24)

```
Job Monitor - Jobs in MSGW Status          Date: mm/dd/yy  hh:mm:ss
Jobs in MSGW:    3  (F5=Refresh)

Opt   Number  User        Job Name     Typ  Subsystem   Fn  Function
────  ──────  ──────────  ──────────  ───  ──────────  ──  ──────────
___   012345  QSYS        QSQSRVR     PJ   QSYSWRK     PG  QSQSRVR
___   023456  BOB4IPGMR   ORDPROC     BCH  QBATCH      PG  ORDPROC
___   034567  JDOE        RPGPGM1     INT  QINTER       PG  RPGPGM1
...
Options: 2=Work With Job  3=Hold Job  4=End (Ctrl)  5=Display Msgs  6=Release
7=Display Job Log  8=End (Immed)  F3=Exit  F5=Refresh  F12=Cancel/Deselect
────────────────────────────── Status messages appear here ─────────────────
```

---

### DDS Record Formats — [`MSGWDSPF`](BOB4IPGMR/QDSPFSRC/MSGWDSPF.DSPF)

| Format | Type | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `MSGSFL` | SFL | One row per MSGW job; `SFOPT` for operator input; `SFQJOB` hidden field holds qualified job name |
| `MSGCTL` | SFLCTL | Page header, date/time, job count (`CTJOBCNT`), column headings. `SFLSIZ(9999) SFLPAG(15)` |
| `FOOTER` | OVERLAY | Fixed function-key legend on lines 22–23; written once, persists via OVERLAY |
| `MSGQSFL` | SFL (message) | `SFLMSGRCD(24)` — displays messages on line 24 |
| `MSGQCTL` | SFLCTL | Controls the message subfile via `IN90` (display) and `IN91` (clear) |

**Key DDS design decisions:**
- **`INDARA`** — indicator area separated from the record buffer; RPG uses a named `DCL-DS` instead of raw `*IN` array
- **`CF03/CF05/CF12`** at file level — function keys map cleanly to named indicators in the `Ind` DS
- **`CTJOBCNT`** is a named output field, so `COLOR(GRN/YLW)` works (colour only applies to named fields, not unnamed constants)
- **`OVERLAY`** on `FOOTER` — the legend never gets cleared by subsequent `EXFMT MSGCTL` calls

---

### RPGLE Program Logic — [`MSGWMON`](BOB4IPGMR/QRPGLESRC/MSGWMON.SQLRPGLE)

**Key declarations:**
```rpg
dcl-s WkRRN  zoned(4:0);   // SFILE RRN — must be declared before file
dcl-f MSGWDSPF workstn sfile(MSGSFL: WkRRN) indds(Ind);
```
The `SFILE(MSGSFL: WkRRN)` keyword is what registers `MSGSFL` as a known subfile format, enabling `write`, `readc`, and `update` on it.

**Main loop:**
```
write FOOTER  →  dou F3Exit { LoadSubfile → exfmt MSGCTL → ProcessOptions }
```

**`LoadSubfile` subroutine** uses `QSYS2.ACTIVE_JOB_INFO()` with a cursor:
```sql
WHERE JOB_STATUS = 'MSGW'
ORDER BY JOB_TYPE, SUBSYSTEM, JOB_USER, JOB_NAME
```
Each row populates a subfile write including the hidden `SFQJOB` field (qualified job name `nnnnnnn/user/jobname`).

**`ProcessOptions` subroutine** uses **`READC MSGSFL`** — reads only rows the operator modified (MDT set), which is more efficient than looping all RRNs.

**Operator actions (option → CL command):**

| Opt | Action | CL Command Issued |
|---|---|---|
| `2` | Work With Job | `WRKJOB JOB(...)` |
| `3` | Hold Job | `HLDJOB JOB(...) DUPJOBOPT(*MSG)` |
| `4` | End Job (Controlled) | `ENDJOB ... OPTION(*CNTRLD) DELAY(30)` |
| `5` | Display Messages | `WRKMSG JOB(...)` |
| `6` | Release Job | `RLSJOB JOB(...) DUPJOBOPT(*MSG)` |
| `7` | Display Job Log | `DSPJOBLOG JOB(...) OUTPUT(*)` |
| `8` | End Job (Immediate) | `ENDJOB ... OPTION(*IMMED)` |

All destructive operations (3, 4, 6, 8) are wrapped in `monitor/on-error` blocks and report results to the **message subfile** via `QMHSNDPM` to `*EXT`.

---

### How to run

```cl
CALL PGM(BOB4IPGMR/MSGWMON)
```

> **Authority note:** The operator's user profile needs `*JOBCTL` special authority to act on jobs owned by other users (HLDJOB, ENDJOB, RLSJOB). The program itself needs no special authority just to display MSGW jobs — `QSYS2.ACTIVE_JOB_INFO` is publicly readable.

data.content:
Good. I can see all three issues clearly now. Let me diagnose each one:

**Issue 1 — "F5=Refresh" text in MSGCTL (line 78):** Remove the `'(F5=Refresh)'` constant from the subfile control record.

**Issue 2 — Footer not showing:** `write FOOTER` is called once *before* the loop. But `EXFMT MSGCTL` performs a full-screen write which clears non-OVERLAY records. `FOOTER` has `OVERLAY` so it *should* persist — the real problem is the **write sequence**: `FOOTER` is written *before* `MSGCTL` is ever written. The OVERLAY mechanism only preserves records that are already on the display *when a subsequent record without OVERLAY is output*. Since `MSGCTL` is written by `EXFMT` *after* `FOOTER`, the `MSGCTL` write clears the display first (it has no OVERLAY), then writes itself — `FOOTER` lines 22-23 would be cleared. The fix: **write `FOOTER` inside the loop, after `LoadSubfile` and before `EXFMT MSGCTL`**, so it is on the screen at the same time. Since `FOOTER` uses `OVERLAY`, it won't clear MSGCTL's content. Then `EXFMT MSGCTL` (no OVERLAY) will clear the screen and write the subfile header — which then erases FOOTER again. 

The correct pattern for OVERLAY footer + subfile: **write FOOTER after EXFMT MSGCTL** is wrong too. The right approach is: `MSGCTL` must also use `OVERLAY`, OR `FOOTER` must be written *after* MSGCTL on every iteration. Since MSGCTL is displayed with `EXFMT` (which writes AND reads), we need to write FOOTER *before* EXFMT so it lands on screen, but MSGCTL (no OVERLAY) clears it.

The correct DDS solution: add `OVERLAY` to `MSGCTL` as well. That way both `FOOTER` and `MSGCTL` use overlay — neither clears the other. We just need to clear the screen once at startup. Alternatively, move the footer constants *into* `MSGCTL` — but that caused issues previously with column layout.

**The cleanest fix:** Add `OVERLAY` to `MSGCTL`. Write FOOTER once before the loop. Each `EXFMT MSGCTL` (with OVERLAY) will not clear the footer lines (22-23) since they don't overlap with MSGCTL's lines (1-21). The screen should be cleared once at startup with a `write` of a blank record, or simply accepted that the first display clears to blank naturally.

**Issue 3 — QCMDEXC error:** The `WkCmd` is declared as `varchar(256)` but `QCMDEXC` prototype takes `char(32702) const`. When passing a `varchar` to a `char const` parameter, RPG pads with blanks to fill 32702 bytes. `WkCmdLen` must be the **actual trimmed length** — and it is (`%len(%trimr(WkCmd))`). However the real problem is that `%len(%trimr(WkCmd))` on a `varchar` returns the current length of the trimmed string, but `QCMDEXC` needs the length of the data *as passed*. Since RPG passes the varchar value padded to `char(32702)`, `WkCmdLen` must match. The `%len(%trimr(WkCmd))` is correct. 

Actually the root cause of the QCMDEXC error is more likely the **qualified job name format**. `WkQualJob` is `char(26)` but a qualified job name is `number(6)/user(10)/name(10)` = **28 characters** (`6+1+10+1+10`). It's declared as `char(26)` — 2 characters too short, causing the job name to be truncated. So `WRKJOB JOB(123456/LONGUSRNM/LONGJOBNA)` gets cut to 26 chars and the command fails.

Let me fix all three issues together:

data.content:
All three issues fixed and both objects recompiled clean. Here is a precise summary of every change made.

---

## Changes Applied

### Fix 1 — Remove `(F5=Refresh)` from the control format

**File:** [`MSGWDSPF`](BOB4IPGMR/QDSPFSRC/MSGWDSPF.DSPF) — `MSGCTL` record

The constant `'(F5=Refresh)'` on line 2 of the subfile control header was removed. The job count field `CTJOBCNT` now stands alone. The F5 reminder already appears on the `FOOTER` record on line 23.

---

### Fix 2 — Footer not showing

**Root cause:** `MSGCTL` had no `OVERLAY` keyword. When `EXFMT MSGCTL` executed, it performed a **full-screen write** that erased everything — including the `FOOTER` that had been written just before it. Even though `FOOTER` uses `OVERLAY`, that only protects it from being cleared *by subsequent OVERLAY writes*; a non-OVERLAY record always clears the whole screen first.

**Fix applied in [`MSGWDSPF`](BOB4IPGMR/QDSPFSRC/MSGWDSPF.DSPF):**
```
     A          R MSGCTL                    SFLCTL(MSGSFL)
                                            OVERLAY          ← added
```

**How it works now:** `FOOTER` (OVERLAY) is written once before the `dou` loop. On every loop iteration, `EXFMT MSGCTL` (now also OVERLAY) repaints only its own lines (1–21). Lines 22–23 occupied by `FOOTER` are **not overlapping** with MSGCTL, so the system leaves them untouched. The footer persists for the entire session.

---

### Fix 3 — `QCMDEXC` error on options 2, 5, 7

**Root cause:** `WkQualJob` was declared `char(26)` but a fully qualified IBM i job name is `number(6) + '/' + user(10) + '/' + name(10)` = **28 characters**. Jobs with 10-character user profiles or job names were silently truncated, producing a malformed job name that QCMDEXC rejected with `CPF1321: Job not found`.

**Fix applied in [`MSGWMON`](BOB4IPGMR/QRPGLESRC/MSGWMON.SQLRPGLE):**
```rpg
// Before (wrong):
dcl-s WkQualJob char(26);

// After (correct):
dcl-s WkQualJob char(28);   // 6+1+10+1+10 = 28
```

---

Passing Less Data Than Required
IBMi 7.6 ILE RPG Programmers Guide.pdf
When a parameter is prototyped, the compiler will check to see that the length is appropriate for the parameter. If the callee has indicated (through documentation or through that prototype) that a parameter can be shorter than the maximum length, you can safely pass shorter parameters.  
Figure 73 on page 211 shows the prototype for QCMDEXC, where the first parameter is defined with OPTIONS(*VARSIZE) meaning that you can pass parameters of different lengths for the first parameter. Note that OPTIONS *VARSIZE can only be specified for a character field, a UCS-2 field, a graphic field, or an array.  
```
*-------------------------------------------------------------*  This prototype for QCMDEXC defines three parameters.  The *  first parameter can be passed character fields of *  different lengths, since it is defined with *VARSIZE. *-------------------------------------------------------------D qcmdexc         PR                  EXTPGM('QCMDEXC') D   cmd                       3000A   OPTIONS(*VARSIZE) CONST D   cmdlen                      15P 5 CONST D                                3A   CONST OPTIONS(*NOPASS) Figure 73. Prototype for System API QCMDEXC with *VARSIZE Parameter
```

---

Leaving Out Parameters
IBMi 7.6 ILE RPG Programmers Guide.pdf
The other way to omit a parameter is to simply leave it out on the call. This must be expected by the called procedure, which means that it must be indicated on the prototype. To indicate that a prototyped  
parameter does not have to be passed on a call, specify the keyword OPTIONS(*NOPASS) on the corresponding parameter definition. Note that all parameters following the first *NOPASS one must also be specified with OPTIONS(*NOPASS).  
You can specify both *NOPASS and *OMIT for the same parameter, in either order, that is, OPTIONS(*NOPASS:*OMIT) or OPTIONS(*OMIT:*NOPASS).  
As an example of OPTIONS(*NOPASS), consider the system API QCMDEXC (Execute Command) which has an optional third parameter. To allow for this parameter, the prototype for QCMDEXC could be written as shown in Figure 69 on page 205.  
```
*-------------------------------------------------------------*  This prototype for QCMDEXC defines three parameters: *   1- a character field that may be shorter in length *      than expected *   2- any numeric field *   3- an optional character field *-------------------------------------------------------------D qcmdexc         PR                  EXTPGM('QCMDEXC') D   cmd                       3000A   OPTIONS(*VARSIZE)  CONST D   cmdlen                      15P 5 CONST D                                3A   CONST OPTIONS(*NOPASS)

Work with Messages  (WRKMSG)
**Where allowed to run:** All environments (*ALL)  
**Threadsafe:** No 

The Work With Messages (WRKMSG) command is used by the display station user to work with messages received at a specified message queue.

Parameter Overview
| Keyword                        | Description                | Choices                                                                                    | Notes                  |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------- |
| [**MSGQ**](#WRKMSG.MSGQ)       | Message queue              | Single values: ***WRKUSR**, *SYSOPR, *USRPRF, *WRKSTNOther values: _Qualified object name_ | Optional, Positional 1 |
| Qualifier 1: Message queue     | _Name_                     |                                                                                            |                        |
| Qualifier 2: Library           | _Name_, ***LIBL**, *CURLIB |                                                                                            |                        |
| [**OUTPUT**](#WRKMSG.OUTPUT)   | Output                     | *****, *PRINT                                                                              | Optional               |
| [**MSGTYPE**](#WRKMSG.MSGTYPE) | Message type               | ***ALL**, *INFO, *INQ, *COPY                                                               | Optional               |
| [**SEV**](#WRKMSG.SEV)         | Severity code filter       | 0-99, **0**, *MSGQ                                                                         | Optional               |
| [**ASTLVL**](#WRKMSG.ASTLVL)   | Assistance level           | ***PRV**, *USRPRF, *BASIC, *INTERMED                                                       | Optional               |


MSGQ
### Message queue (MSGQ)

Specifies the message queue from which messages are shown. 

**Note:** The special values *WRKSTN, *WRKUSR, *USRPRF, and *SYSOPR should be specified for this parameter only when you are in an interactive job. 

**Single values** 

***WRKUSR**

Messages from the work station's message queue and the current user's user profile message queue are shown. 

***SYSOPR**

Messages from the system operator message queue (QSYSOPR) are shown. 

***WRKSTN**

Messages from the work station's message queue are shown. 

***USRPRF**

Messages from the current user profile message queue are shown. 

**Qualifier 1: Message queue** 

**_name_**

Specify the name of the message queue from which messages are shown. 

**Qualifier 2: Library** 

***LIBL**

All libraries in the library list for the current thread are searched until the first match is found. 

***CURLIB**

The current library for the job is used to locate the message queue. If no current library entry exists in the library list, QGPL is used. 

**_name_**

Specify the library where the message queue is located.


Qualifier 1: Message queue



Qualifier 2: Library



OUTPUT
### Output (OUTPUT)

Specifies whether the output from the command is displayed at the requesting work station or printed with the job's spooled output. 

*****

The output is shown (if requested by an interactive job) or printed with the job's spooled output (if requested by a batch job). Immediate messages and predefined messages are truncated to 105 characters when printed. 

***PRINT**

The output is printed with the job's spooled output. 

When the output is printed, two lines are printed for each message. The second line contains the following information: 

* Qualified job name of the job that sent the message. This consists of the following three fields:  
  * Job name
  * User name
  * Job number
* Name of the program that sent the message
* Instruction number in program that sent the message. For non-program message queues this is always zeroes.
* The date and time the message was sent.
* The name of the user profile that the thread was running under when the message was sent.


MSGTYPE
### Message type (MSGTYPE)

Specifies the type of messages in the message queue that are shown. 

***ALL**

All messages that are in the message queue are shown. 

***INFO**

Only informational messages (those not requiring a reply) are shown. 

***INQ**

Only inquiry messages (those requiring a reply) are shown. 

***COPY**

A copy of each sender's message that was sent to another message queue and required a reply is shown.


SEV
### Severity code filter (SEV)

Specifies the lowest severity code value that a message can have and be shown. If the message's severity code is lower than the value specified here, the message is not shown. 

**0**

All messages in the specified message queue are shown. 

***MSGQ**

All messages having a severity code greater than or equal to the severity code specified for the message queue are shown. 

**_severity-code_**

Specify the lowest severity code value that a message can have and still be shown. Valid values range from 00 through 99\.


ASTLVL
### Assistance level (ASTLVL)

Specifies which user interface to display. 

***PRV**

The previous user interface used is displayed. 

***USRPRF**

The user interface stored in the current user profile is used. 

***BASIC**

The Work with Messages display is shown. This user interface separates messages into two categories: 1) messages requiring a reply and 2) messages not requiring a reply. New messages are shown at the top of each message list. 

***INTERMED**

The Display Messages display is shown.


Examples
WRKMSG

This command displays all messages from the requester's work station message queue and user profile message queue. Messages needing a reply are displayed first, followed by messages not needing a reply. Messages are displayed from newest to oldest.

data.content:
Two problems confirmed:

1. **`QCMDEXC` prototype missing `OPTIONS(*VARSIZE)`** — Without it, RPG always passes a `char(32702)` buffer regardless of the actual command length, while `WkCmdLen` contains only the short trimmed length. QCMDEXC receives a length that doesn't match the actual bytes it can read, causing the error.

2. **`WRKMSG JOB(...)` is wrong** — `WRKMSG` takes a **message queue name** (`MSGQ` parameter), not a job name. To display messages for another job you use `WRKMSG MSGQ(jobname)` pointing to that job's external message queue, which is only accessible if that queue exists as a named object. The correct command to view messages for a specific job is **`WRKJOB JOB(...) OPTION(*MSG)`** or simply show the job's call message queue. The right command is **`DSPJOBLOG`** for the log, and for the actual inquiry messages waiting: **`WRKMSG MSGQ(jobname)`** won't work generically. The correct operator action to view and reply to MSGW messages is `WRKJOB JOB(qualified-name)` then option 10 (Display job log) or directly use `DSPMSG MSGQ(jobname)`. Actually the simplest correct approach: use **`WRKJOB JOB(...)`** with no option — the operator gets the full Work With Job menu and can select messages themselves.

Let me fix both issues now — only the prototype and the option-5 command:

data.content:
I can see the problem clearly now. Look at the option 3 error message:

> `Hold failed: 327961/BOB4IPGMR/327961/BOB4. Check job log.`

The qualified job name is **corrupted** — `327961/BOB4IPGMR/327961/BOB4` instead of `327961/BOB4IPGMR/JOBNAME`. The job number is being repeated and the name is truncated. This is the `SFQJOB` field being built incorrectly.

Also `String '  WRKJOB J' contains a character that is not valid` — there are **two leading spaces** in the command string. That means `WkCmd` starts with spaces, which means `WkCmd` is NOT being assigned correctly — it's retaining old content because `WkCmd` is `varchar` and the assignment is concatenating into a dirty field, OR more likely the `%trimr(WkQualJob)` is including a special character.

Let me look at `SFQJOB` — it's `char(28)` in the DDS but the `WkQualJob` assignment is `char(28)`. The problem is `SFQJOB = WkQualJob` copies all 28 bytes including trailing spaces. So `%trimr(WkQualJob)` should strip them. But the job number field `JobRow.JobNumber` is `varchar(6)` — `JOB_NUMBER` from ACTIVE_JOB_INFO returns a 6-digit zero-padded number like `327961`. That looks fine.

Wait — re-read the error: `327961/BOB4IPGMR/327961/BOB4`. The user name is `BOB4IPGMR` (9 chars) and the job name appears to be truncated to `BOB4` (4 chars). That means `SFQJOB` which is `char(28)` only holds `327961/BOB4IPGMR/327961/BOB4` = 28 characters exactly — the job name `BOB4IPGMR` continued right after the second `/` taking up positions 19-27 but then truncating the actual job name because the buffer ran out.

**The real bug:** `SFQJOB` in the DDS is `28A` (28 characters) and the hidden field `WkQualJob` is `char(28)`. But when we copy `SFQJOB` (28 chars) to `WkQualJob` (28 chars), trailing spaces are included. Then `%trimr(WkQualJob)` works fine. BUT the *build* of SFQJOB itself is wrong:

`SFQJOB = %trimr(JobRow.JobNumber) + '/' + %trimr(JobRow.JobUser) + '/' + %trimr(JobRow.JobName)`

For job `327961/BOB4IPGMR/SOMEJOBNAM`:
- `%trimr('327961') = '327961'` (6)
- `'/'` (1) 
- `%trimr('BOB4IPGMR') = 'BOB4IPGMR'` (9)
- `'/'` (1)
- `%trimr('SOMEJOBNAM') = 'SOMEJOBNAM'` (10)
= total 27 chars — fits in 28 ✓

But for `327961/BOB4IPGMR/327961/BOB4` — that's the JOB_NAME column returning `327961` and `BOB4`? No. Looking more carefully — `JOB_NAME` from ACTIVE_JOB_INFO returns the **full qualified job name** (`number/user/name`) as a single 28-char column. But we're also selecting `JOB_USER` and `JOB_NUMBER` separately. So `JobRow.JobName` is already `327961/BOB4IPGMR/JOBNAME` — the full qualified name! We're then concatenating number + `/` + user + `/` + **full-qualified-name**, creating the double encoding.

data.content:
Now I have the complete picture. Here are **all the bugs in one place**:

1. **`SFQJOB` built wrong** — `JobRow.JobName` IS already `number/user/name`. The line `SFQJOB = number + '/' + user + '/' + JobName` double-encodes it.
2. **`SFJOBNAM` shows wrong value** — It was set to `%char(JobRow.JobName)` which shows the full `number/user/name` string instead of just the short name.
3. **`WkCmd` starts with spaces** — Because `WkCmd` is `varchar` and the `+` concatenation in RPG with `varchar` works fine, but `%trimr(WkQualJob)` — since `WkQualJob = SFQJOB` copies all 28 bytes from the `char(28)` field — if the qualified name is shorter than 28 the trailing spaces stay, but `%trimr` handles those. The leading spaces in `'  WRKJOB J'` come from **`WkCmd` itself retaining old content** — actually no, the real issue is the corrupted `WkQualJob` making a command like `WRKJOB JOB(327961/BOB4IPGMR/327961/BOB4)` where the closing `)` falls after position 28 of WkQualJob and gets cut, so the command string has no closing `)`.

The single fix: **change the SQL to select the short job name separately** and **assign `SFQJOB = JobRow.JobName` directly**.

data.content:
Compiled clean. Here is the precise root cause and every change made.

---

## Root Cause

`ACTIVE_JOB_INFO.JOB_NAME` returns the **fully qualified job name** — `number/user/name` — as a single 28-character value. The code was treating it as only the *short* job name and manually rebuilding the qualified name by concatenating it with `JOB_NUMBER` and `JOB_USER`:

```rpg
// OLD — Double-encodes the job name:
SFQJOB = %trimr(JobRow.JobNumber) + '/' +   // '327961'
         %trimr(JobRow.JobUser)   + '/' +   // 'BOB4IPGMR'
         %trimr(JobRow.JobName);             // '327961/BOB4IPGMR/MYJOB' ← already full!
// Result stored in char(28): '327961/BOB4IPGMR/327961/BOB4'  (truncated!)
```

This produced a corrupt job name like `327961/BOB4IPGMR/327961/BOB4`, which caused every CL command to fail with *"String contains invalid character"* and *"matching parenthesis not found"* because the closing `)` was past position 28 and got dropped.

---

## Changes Made — [`MSGWMON`](BOB4IPGMR/QRPGLESRC/MSGWMON.SQLRPGLE)

### 1. Added `JobShortName` to `JobRow` DS
```rpg
dcl-ds JobRow qualified;
  JobName      varchar(28);   // Full qualified name: number/user/name
  JobShortName varchar(10);   // Short name only — for the display column
  ...
end-ds;
```

### 2. SQL cursor now selects the short name via `SUBSTR`
```sql
SELECT
  JOB_NAME,                                         -- already 'nbr/usr/name'
  SUBSTR(JOB_NAME,
    LOCATE('/', JOB_NAME, LOCATE('/', JOB_NAME)+1)+1) AS JOB_NAME_SHORT,
  JOB_USER, JOB_NUMBER, ...
```

### 3. Subfile populate — `SFQJOB` assigned directly, `SFJOBNAM` uses short name
```rpg
// BEFORE (wrong):
SFJOBNAM = %char(JobRow.JobName);                 // showed 'nbr/usr/name'
SFQJOB   = number + '/' + user + '/' + JobName;  // double-encoded

// AFTER (correct):
SFJOBNAM = %char(JobRow.JobShortName);            // shows 'MYJOB'
SFQJOB   = %char(JobRow.JobName);                 // '327961/BOB4IPGMR/MYJOB'
```

### 4. `WkQualJob` changed from `char(28)` to `varchar(28)`
```rpg
dcl-s WkQualJob varchar(28);   // varchar — no trailing-space trimming needed
```
And in `ProcessOptions`, assigned cleanly:
```rpg
WkQualJob = %trimr(SFQJOB);    // strip trailing spaces from char(28) field
WkCmd     = 'WRKJOB JOB(' + WkQualJob + ')';  // no %trimr needed on varchar
WkCmdLen  = %len(WkCmd);       // exact length of the varchar value
```

data.content:
The RPG code looks correct. The error `String '  DSPJOBLO'` has **two leading spaces** — this cannot come from string concatenation in RPG. The issue is that `WkCmd` is `varchar(512)` and the string literal `'DSPJOBLOG JOB('` is being stored correctly. But two leading spaces mean `WkCmd` contains `'  DSPJOBLOG JOB(...)'`.

**The real cause:** `WkCmd` is passed to `QCMDEXC` with `OPTIONS(*VARSIZE)` — RPG passes the **full current length of the varchar variable**, which is 512 bytes (the declared max), not the actual data length. `%len(WkCmd)` on a `varchar` returns the **current data length** (correct), but `OPTIONS(*VARSIZE)` passes the **declared max length** (512) — the two conflict.

Wait — let me re-examine. With `OPTIONS(*VARSIZE)` on a `varchar` parameter, RPG strips the 2-byte length prefix and passes the data bytes only — the length it passes is `%len(WkCmd)` (the current data length). But the `CmdLen` parameter is set to `%len(WkCmd)` which is also the current data length. Those should match.

Actually the problem is different. `WkCmd` is `varchar(512)`. When you assign `WkCmd = 'DSPJOBLOG JOB(' + WkQualJob + ') OUTPUT(*)'`, RPG assigns the concatenated string. But `%len(WkCmd)` returns the **current length** of the varchar data. With `OPTIONS(*VARSIZE)` the compiler passes the **address of the varchar data portion** (after the 2-byte length prefix) AND the actual current length. So this should work.

Let me look more carefully at the error message: `String '  DSPJOBLO'` — **two spaces then DSPJOBLO**. The string shown is the *first 10 characters* of the command. Two leading spaces means positions 1-2 are spaces. Where do those spaces come from?

**Found it:** `WkCmd` is `varchar(512)`. The QCMDEXC prototype's `Cmd` parameter is `varchar(32702) options(*varsize)`. When passing a `varchar` argument to a `varchar(*varsize)` parameter, RPG passes it as a **fixed character string** (char) of the varchar's **declared maximum length** — 512 bytes — padded with the current data followed by blanks. The `CmdLen` is only the trimmed length, but QCMDEXC reads the first `CmdLen` bytes starting from position 1 of the 512-byte buffer. That should be fine.

**But wait** — `WkCmd` declared as `varchar(512)` has a **2-byte length prefix** in memory. When RPG passes `varchar` to a `char OPTIONS(*VARSIZE)` or `varchar OPTIONS(*VARSIZE)` parameter, the behavior depends on whether the receiving parameter is `char` or `varchar`. With `varchar(32702) options(*varsize)` as the prototype parameter, RPG passes the **varchar value directly including its 2-byte length header** — so QCMDEXC sees 2 bytes of binary length data as the first two characters — which would look like spaces or garbage.

**This is the root cause:** When passing a `varchar` variable to a `varchar OPTIONS(*VARSIZE)` prototype parameter, the system passes the raw varchar including its internal 2-byte length prefix as part of the data. QCMDEXC then reads those 2 bytes as the start of the command — hence `'  DSPJOBLO'` (the 2 length bytes look like two spaces).

**The fix:** The QCMDEXC `Cmd` parameter should be declared as **`char OPTIONS(*VARSIZE)`**, not `varchar OPTIONS(*VARSIZE)`. And `WkCmd` should remain `varchar` for easy building, but be passed via a `char` intermediate or simply use `%char(WkCmd)`. OR — keep `WkCmd` as `varchar` and pass `%str(WkCmd)` — but the simplest correct fix per IBM documentation is: declare `Cmd` as `char OPTIONS(*VARSIZE)` in the prototype and pass the `varchar` variable directly (RPG auto-converts varchar → char for the call).

Let me verify with IBM docs first:

Results showing 4 results from search "QCMDEXC prototype RPG varchar char OPTIONS VARSIZE passing varchar command string correct way":

---

CALLP (Call a Prototyped Procedure or Program)
IBMi%207.6%20ILE%20RPG%20Reference.pdf
```
*..1....+....2....+....3....+....4....+....5....+....6....+....7...+.... *-------------------------------------------------------------*  This prototype for QCMDEXC defines two parameters: *   1- a character field that may be shorter in length *      than expected *   2- any numeric field *-------------------------------------------------------------D qcmdexc         PR                  extpgm('QCMDEXC') D   cmd                        200A   options(*varsize) const D   cmdlen                      15P 5 const /FREE qcmdexc ('WRKSPLF' : %size ('WRKSPLF')); /END-FREE Figure 276. Calling a Prototyped Program Using CALLP * The prototype for the procedure has an array parameter. D proc            pr D   parm                        10a   dim(5) * An array to pass to the procedure D array           s             10a   dim(5) * Call the procedure, passing the array C                   callp     proc (array) Figure 277. Passing an array parameter using CALLP
```  
The following example of CALLP is from the service program example in Rational Development Studio for i: ILE RPG Programmer's Guide . CvtToHex is a procedure in a service program created to hold conversion routines. CvtToHex converts an input string to its hexadecimal form. The prototyped calls are to the ILE CEE API, CEEDOD (Retrieve Operational Descriptor). It is used to determine the length of the input string. Figure 278. Calling a Prototyped Procedure Using CALLP  
<!-- image -->  
```
*-----------------------------------------------------------------* * Other fields used by the program                                * *-----------------------------------------------------------------* D HexDigits       C                   CONST('0123456789ABCDEF') D IntDs           DS D   IntNum                       5I 0 INZ(0) D   IntChar                      1    OVERLAY(IntNum:2) D HexDs           DS D   HexC1                        1 D   HexC2                        1 D InChar          S              1 D Pos             S              5P 0 D HexPos          S              5P 0 /FREE //-------------------------------------------------------------// // Use the operational descriptors to determine the lengths of // // the parameters that were passed.

---

Passing Less Data Than Required
IBMi 7.6 ILE RPG Programmers Guide.pdf
When a parameter is prototyped, the compiler will check to see that the length is appropriate for the parameter. If the callee has indicated (through documentation or through that prototype) that a parameter can be shorter than the maximum length, you can safely pass shorter parameters.  
Figure 73 on page 211 shows the prototype for QCMDEXC, where the first parameter is defined with OPTIONS(*VARSIZE) meaning that you can pass parameters of different lengths for the first parameter. Note that OPTIONS *VARSIZE can only be specified for a character field, a UCS-2 field, a graphic field, or an array.  
```
*-------------------------------------------------------------*  This prototype for QCMDEXC defines three parameters.  The *  first parameter can be passed character fields of *  different lengths, since it is defined with *VARSIZE. *-------------------------------------------------------------D qcmdexc         PR                  EXTPGM('QCMDEXC') D   cmd                       3000A   OPTIONS(*VARSIZE) CONST D   cmdlen                      15P 5 CONST D                                3A   CONST OPTIONS(*NOPASS) Figure 73. Prototype for System API QCMDEXC with *VARSIZE Parameter
```

---

Example 1: Call a program
RPG%20tutorial%20for%20experienced%20programmers.pdf
A common program to call is QCMDEXC. This program runs a system command.  
```
dcl-pr qcmdexc extpgm('QCMDEXC'); theCmd char(3000) const; cmdLen packed(15 : 5) const; dbcs char(3) const options(*nopass); end-pr; dcl-s cmd varchar(100); cmd = 'DSPJOB OUTPUT(*PRINT)'; qcmdexc (cmd : %len(cmd)); qcmdexc ('WRKSPLF' : 7); return;
```

---

Bonus features in this example:
RPG%20tutorial%20for%20experienced%20programmers.pdf
- The program name in the EXTPGM keyword is case-sensitive. The system would not be able to find the program if the RPG program specified 'QcmdExc' in the EXTPGM keyword.
- The CONST keyword indicates that the called program does not modify the parameter. When CONST is specified, the passed parameter does not have to exactly match the type and length on the prototype. If the type and length don't match, the RPG compiler creates a temporary variable of the required type and pass that temporary to the called program. Coding CONST also allows literals and expressions to be passed as parameters.
- The call that uses the prototype is coded with the parameters in parentheses. The parameter separator is a colon, not a comma, as is more usual in other languages.
- The %len built-in function returns the current length of the varying-length variable "cmd".  
Note: If the RPG prototype name is the same as the actual program name, you can just code EXTPGM with no parameter. The RPG compiler uppercases the prototype name to determine the actual program name. Here is an alternate version of the QCMDEXC prototype.  
```
dcl-pr qcmdexc extpgm; theCmd char(3000) const; cmdLen packed(15 : 5) const; dbcs char(3) const options(*nopass); end-pr;
```
